journal.title: Field notes from people who just got back

items.a: Most stays and experiences cancel free up to 48 hours before they start — look for the “Free cancellation” line. Packages cancel free until 30 days before departure; after that, 50% is refundable until 14 days out. The exact terms are on every booking before you pay.
Payments go through a PCI-DSS certified provider, so we never see or store your card number. You get written confirmation from us and from the place you’re staying.
No. Tap the heart on anything and it’s saved on this device. When you’re ready, a planner sends your trip by email.
The nightly price includes VAT and service fees. The only thing you might pay locally is a city tourist tax, and we flag it on the stay when it applies.
Within an hour, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. WhatsApp is usually quickest.

porto48.title: Porto in 48 hours, mostly on foot
porto48.dek: Three hills, two bridges, one very good francesinha, and the side streets most walking tours skip.
porto48.alt: Porto’s Dom Luís I bridge at sunset
body: Start high and walk down. Take the funicular to Batalha before nine, while the bakeries are still pulling trays out, and follow Rua das Flores towards the river. Every second door is a shop that has sold the same thing for ninety years.
Cross the Dom Luís I bridge on the upper deck at golden hour, then have dinner on the Gaia side, where the port lodges are. Book one tasting, not three — the good ones take their time.
On day two, catch the 500 bus to Foz and walk back along the river. It is eight kilometres, it is flat, and it is the best way to understand how the city meets the Atlantic.

japanTrains.title: Japan’s slow trains, and why we prefer them
japanTrains.dek: Skip the shinkansen for a day. Local lines go where bullet trains don’t — and the views are worth the extra hours.
japanTrains.alt: Looking out of a Japanese train window at a village and green hills
body: The bullet train is a marvel, but it is a tunnel with seats. Local lines — the Gonō, the Sanin, the Iiyama — run along coastlines and rice terraces at a pace that lets you notice things.
Our planners build at least one slow-rail day into every Japan trip. Bring a bento from the station, sit on the sea side, and let the timetable decide the afternoon.
A rail pass rarely pays for itself on these routes. We will tell you honestly when it does, and when individual tickets are cheaper.

cdmxBreakfast.title: Mexico City, one breakfast at a time
cdmxBreakfast.dek: Chilaquiles in Roma, tamales in Coyoacán, and a pan dulce ranking we will defend.
cdmxBreakfast.alt: People walking past a stone building on a Mexico City street
body: Mexico City is a breakfast city. Lunch is late and long, dinner is optional, but breakfast is a ritual — and every neighbourhood does it differently.
In Roma, order chilaquiles verdes with a fried egg and don’t share. In Coyoacán, follow the queue to the tamal cart outside the market and point at whatever the person before you ordered.
Our ranking of conchas is final and not open to discussion. Ask your planner for the list — they will only share it in person.

tbilisiNow.title: Tbilisi, before the crowds work it out
tbilisiNow.dek: Sulphur baths, natural wine and a city that still feels like it’s being discovered.
tbilisiNow.alt: Tbilisi rooftops under an orange evening sky
body: Tbilisi sits in a valley that traps the evening light, and most of the old town is still lived in rather than staged. Book a private room at the sulphur baths in Abanotubani — an hour is enough.
Georgian wine has been made in clay qvevri for eight thousand years. A good wine bar here will pour you something orange, unfiltered and unlike anything at home.
Go in late spring or early autumn. Summer is hot, winter is beautiful but grey, and the shoulder months are when the city is at its most generous.
